# AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts), NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5 — what the control actually requires

## 1. Bottom line

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, control AC-7, requires **no specific number of consecutive invalid logon attempts, no specific counting time period, and no specific lockout duration.** All three are Organization-Defined Parameters (ODPs), printed in the control as bracketed `[Assignment: organization-defined ...]` placeholders. What AC-7 requires is that the organization (a) define a limit and a counting period, (b) define and configure one or more automatic responses when the limit is exceeded, and (c) enforce both. Any answer of the form "AC-7 requires N attempts within M minutes with an X-minute lockout" is not AC-7; no such figure exists in the publication.

Applies to the base control and its enhancements as published in Rev. 5 (including the 5.2.0 minor release of 27 Aug 2025, whose change list — SA-15(13), SA-24, SI-02(07), SI-07(12), discussion updates to SA-04, SA-05, SA-08, SA-08(14), SI-02, SI-02(05), related-control updates — does not touch AC-7).

## 2. The control text, verbatim

Source: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/nist.sp.800-53r5.pdf (fetched 2026-11-25T04:59:28Z, sha256 fc63bcd61715)

> **AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS**
> **Control:**
> a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
> b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined action]] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded.

Cross-checked, character-for-character on the operative wording, in three independent renderings:

- Rev. 5 controls workbook, https://csrc.nist.gov/files/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final/docs/sp800-53r5-controls.xlsx (sha256 6fc1c2414396), row `AC-7 Unsuccessful Logon Attempts`.
- Rev. 5 public draft, https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-53r5-draft.pdf (sha256 d1fd2107db9d), lines 1874–1882 (draft hyphenates "time-period"; final does not).
- Mirror at https://nist-sp-800-53-r5.bsafes.com/docs/3-1-access-control/ac-7-unsuccessful-logon-attamps/ (sha256 f9630cd5ebc4).

## 3. Ask-by-ask

| Ask | Where it lives in AC-7 | ODP identifier (SP 800-53A Rev. 5) | Value NIST fixes |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 — number of consecutive invalid logon attempts | AC-7a, "a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number]" | AC-07_ODP[01] | None — organization-defined |
| 2 — time period for counting those attempts | AC-7a, "during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]" | AC-07_ODP[02] | None — organization-defined |
| 3 — lockout duration | AC-7b, "lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]" — and only **if** that selection is chosen from five options | AC-07_ODP[04] (with the selection itself at AC-07_ODP[03]) | None — organization-defined; and a lockout is not mandatory in kind |

Note on ask 3 specifically: AC-7b is a *selection*, not an assignment. The organization picks one or more of: timed lock, administrator-released lock, delay algorithm, administrator notification, or another defined action. A duration therefore has no referent at all unless the timed-lock option is selected; if it is, the duration is still an organizational choice.

## 4. Corroboration: the assessor's side (SP 800-53A Rev. 5)

Source: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/SpecialPublications/NIST.SP.800-53Ar5.pdf (sha256 75665570048b), AC-07 assessment objective, Chapter Four p. 81:

> AC-07_ODP[01] the number of consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user allowed during a time period **is defined**;
> AC-07_ODP[02] the time period to which the number of consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user is limited **is defined**;
> AC-07_ODP[03] one or more of the following PARAMETER VALUES is/are selected: {lock the account or node for <AC-07_ODP[04] time period>; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per <AC-07_ODP[05] delay algorithm>; notify system administrator; take other <AC-07_ODP[06] action>};
> AC-07_ODP[04] time period for an account or node to be locked **is defined (if selected)**;

This is decisive for the question as asked: the assessment question is *whether the organization defined the value*, not whether the value equals a NIST number. There is no NIST number to compare against.

## 5. What NIST does say about lockout behaviour (discussion, not requirement)

From the AC-7 discussion, as fetched from the publication and from the MITRE CTID reproduction (sha256 702cdc410ff3):

> Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period.

> Automatically unlocking an account after a specified period of time is generally not permitted. However, exceptions may be required based on operational mission or need.

Two things follow. First, both sentences are *discussion* text — guidance, not mandate — and they pull in opposite directions (timed lockouts are usual; automatic unlock is generally not permitted). The tension is resolved by the organization's denial-of-service risk analysis and by the AC-7b selection: an administrator-released lock or a delay algorithm sidesteps it. Second, neither sentence carries a number. The word "lockout" appears in discussion prose; a lockout *duration* value appears nowhere.

## 6. Enhancements — also numberless

- **AC-7(1) Automatic Account Lock** — withdrawn in Rev. 5, incorporated into AC-7 (bsafes mirror, sha256 f9630cd5ebc4). Anyone citing "AC-7(1)" as the lockout authority is citing a withdrawn enhancement.
- **AC-7(2) Purge or Wipe Mobile Device** — "after [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive, unsuccessful device logon attempts."
- **AC-7(3) Biometric Attempt Limiting** — "Limit the number of unsuccessful biometric logon attempts to [Assignment: organization-defined number]."
- **AC-7(4) Use of Alternate Authentication Factor** — organization-defined factors, number and time period.

## 7. Baselines add no values

AC-7 appears in the LOW, MODERATE and HIGH baselines (Appendix D, Table D-1: "AC-7 Unsuccessful Logon Attempts — AC-7 AC-7 AC-7"; draft baselines markup, sha256 bba84ffcac41). Baselines select controls; they do not fill ODPs. Selecting AC-7 at every impact level means the organization must complete the ODPs at every impact level — it does not supply them.

## 8. What this means in practice (the engineering consequence)

1. **Complete the ODPs in policy, not in code comments.** The values belong in the access control policy (AC-1) and the system security plan; the technical configuration must match them, because that is exactly what SP 800-53A examines (policy, procedures, configuration settings, logs).
2. **Shape of the completed control statement** (illustrative placeholders only — these are *not* NIST values and I am deliberately not inventing numbers): "Enforce a limit of `<N>` consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during `<T1>`; and automatically lock the account or node for `<T2>` when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded."
3. **Choose the response deliberately.** Because AC-7b is a selection, document which option(s) you implemented and why. A timed lock is the availability-hostile choice; a delay algorithm plus administrator notification often satisfies the control with less denial-of-service exposure.
4. **Derive `<N>`, `<T1>`, `<T2>` from your own risk analysis** — online guessing exposure, account-lockout-as-DoS risk, help-desk unlock cost, whether MFA is enforced (which changes the guessing economics). Record the rationale so an assessor can see the value was defined, not defaulted.
5. **Do not import numbers from elsewhere.** Specific lockout numbers circulate from operating-system and directory-service defaults and from other NIST publications (e.g., SP 800-63B's rate-limiting guidance, which is a different document with a different scope and was not consulted in this grounding). None of them is AC-7. If the question is "what does AC-7 require", the only correct answer is "the organization-defined values you documented and enforced."

## 9. Searches performed, and what they establish

All three asks were searched against the full text of every page read (see the `not_stated` entries for page names, character counts, hashes and exact search strings):

- **Ask 1** — "number of consecutive invalid logon attempts" / "consecutive invalid logon attempts" / "invalid logon attempts": absent from the draft baselines markup, the ePACS overlay, the CSRC landing page and SP 800-53A Rev. 5. Where the concept does appear in the control, it appears as the placeholder `[Assignment: organization-defined number]`.
- **Ask 2** — "time period" / "specified time period" / "time period specified by the organization": absent from the draft baselines markup and the CSRC landing page; in the control it appears only as `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]`.
- **Ask 3** — "lockout duration" / "account lockout duration" / "duration of the lockout": absent from all pages read, including the complete 492-page Rev. 5 publication and the 733-page SP 800-53A. The duration concept survives only as the placeholder `[Assignment: organization-defined time period]` inside the optional timed-lock selection.

No product, sum or power of figures stated on these pages yields any of the three values — there are no constituent figures to combine. The answer to each ask is therefore that the publication states no value, and no figure is offered for any of them.

CODATA 2022 and CODATA 2018 recommended values of the Rydberg constant R∞ (infinite nuclear mass)

1. CODATA 2022 recommended value
   R∞ = 10 973 731.568 157 m^-1
   Standard uncertainty u(R∞) = 0.000 012 m^-1
   Relative standard uncertainty u_r(R∞) = 1.1 × 10^-12
   Concise form: 10 973 731.568 157(12) m^-1

2. CODATA 2018 recommended value that the 2022 adjustment replaced
   R∞ = 10 973 731.568 160 m^-1
   Standard uncertainty u(R∞) = 0.000 012 m^-1
   Relative standard uncertainty u_r(R∞) = 1.1 × 10^-12
   Concise form: 10 973 731.568 160(12) m^-1

Comparison
   ΔR∞ = R∞(2022) - R∞(2018) = -0.000 003 m^-1 = -3 × 10^-6 m^-1
   In units of the 2018 standard uncertainty: Δ/u(2018) = -0.25
   Relative change: Δ/R∞(2018) ≈ -2.7 × 10^-13
   The shift is well within the quoted one-sigma uncertainty; it is a consequence of the 2022 adjustment, not a contradiction between the two recommended sets.

Notes on interpretation and sourcing
   - R∞ here is the Rydberg constant for an ininitely heavy nucleus, not the reduced-mass Rydberg constant for hydrogen, R_H.
   - Standard uncertainty means the one-sigma standard uncertainty as published by CODATA; no expansion factor (k = 2) is applied.
   - The unit m^-1 is cycles or periods per meter, per the NIST footnote on the Rydberg constant page.

answer:
CLASS R BOND REQUIREMENTS IN NASA-STD-4003A — WHAT THE STANDARD ACTUALLY SAYS
(Reference used: NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, revalidated 03-13-2026, plus the historical NASA-STD-4003A text. Both carry identical Class R technical content; Change 1 adds the [EBR nn] requirement tagging.)

============================================================
BOTTOM LINE (answers the designer's question)
============================================================
There is no maximum RF impedance, in ohms at a stated frequency, for a Class R joint in NASA-STD-4003A. The standard contains no ohms-at-a-frequency figure for Class R at all, and no test frequency. A designer asking for 'the Class R RF impedance limit' is asking for a number that this document does not contain.

What the standard does contain is a two-part requirement:
  (a) a DESIGN requirement — the bond path and every joint in it must have low enough inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, to prevent interference at the program's frequencies of interest; and
  (b) one NUMERIC limit — 2.5 milliohms maximum dc resistance across each joint in the path.

Item (b) is a dc resistance, not an RF impedance, and the standard's own appendix says so explicitly. If a program needs a numeric RF impedance criterion, it must derive and impose it itself; NASA-STD-4003A will not supply it.

============================================================
1. VERBATIM REQUIREMENT TEXT — CLASS R
============================================================
Definition (Appendix A): “CLASS R — class of bond for radio frequency current.”

§4.1.4 Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R) — “The intent of Class R bonding is to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical equipment at radio frequencies.”

§4.1.4a [EBR 20] — “All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.”

§4.1.4b [EBR 21] — “All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.”

§4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22] — “The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.”

§4.1.4c [EBR 23] — “The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle.”

Summary table entry for Class R in the standard:
  BOND REQMT: “Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort.”
  DC BOND RESISTANCE REQMT: “Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required.”
  FREQ. REQMT: High.   CURRENT REQMT: Low.

============================================================
2. WHAT IS *NOT* IN THE STANDARD (explicitly checked)
============================================================
- No maximum RF impedance in ohms. Not at 1 MHz, 30 MHz, 100 MHz, or anywhere else.
- No stated test frequency or frequency band. EBR 21 says only “the frequencies of interest”, which is a program-defined quantity.
- No surface-transfer-impedance limit and no transfer-impedance test method.
- No impedance-vs-frequency curve or table for bonds.
- No numeric RF limit is inherited from the referenced documents either; SAE-ARP-1870 and NASA-STD-6012/6016 are cited for method and corrosion control, not for a Class R impedance value.

Appendix B states the position directly:
  “The basic requirement is to have low impedance at the frequency or frequencies of interest. The value of this impedance … is not defined.”
  “The impedance of an acceptable bond may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. The resistance is overshadowed by the inductive reactance of the configuration.”

============================================================
3. WHY THE 2.5 MILLIOHM FIGURE IS NOT AN RF CRITERION
============================================================
The standard says this itself, twice, and a designer must not conflate the two:
  “There is no RF design basis for the historical 2.5-milliohm requirement except to ensure a good metal-to-metal contact that can be expected to be consistent.”
  “The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. Also, extra effort need not be made just to satisfy the dc requirement if the RF impedance is much higher due to the inductance of the configuration. Look at the whole configuration to get the lowest impedance possible at the frequencies of interest to produce a good RF bond.”

Origin of the number: MIL-B-5087B class R, quoted as “a direct current resistance of less than 2.5 milliohms from enclosure to structure.” NASA-STD-4003A carries the historical figure forward as a workmanship/consistency control, not as an RF performance prediction.

============================================================
4. VALUES THAT ARE *NOT* NASA-STD-4003A CLASS R (distractors)
============================================================
These appear in the NASA technical reference literature and are commonly mis-attributed. They belong to other documents and must not be quoted as this standard's Class R requirement:
  - MIL-STD-1310G: quoted in the NASA reference as “less than 25 ohms at 30 MHz for all electronic equipment to structure.” (Verify the exact unit against the primary MIL-STD-1310G text before using it in a program document — the secondary source's wording is ambiguous between ohms and milliohms.)
  - SSP-30245: quoted as “less than 100 milliohms at 1 MHz, but it does not include the impedance of straps where they are used.”
  - MIL-STD-464: “For Navy aircraft and Army aircraft applications, the EMI bonds shall have a dc resistance of 2.5 milliohms or less across each joint between the subsystem or equipment enclosure and the system ground reference.” (dc, and service-specific.)
If the program wants a frequency-specific number, it must adopt one of these by tailoring and say so — it does not come from NASA-STD-4003A.

============================================================
5. REQUIREMENT / VERIFICATION MATRIX FOR A CLASS R JOINT
============================================================
R-1 (EBR 20)  Enclosure-to-structure low-impedance path exists.        Verify: analysis + inspection of bond schedule.
R-2 (EBR 21)  Path and joints low inductance and low impedance,         Verify: analysis of path L and C, resonance check
              including resonances, at frequencies of interest.          against the program's frequency list; test on
                                                                        representative coupons where practical.
R-3 (EBR 22)  dc resistance across each joint <= 2.5 milliohms.          Verify: 4-wire dc measurement, sample bonds per
                                                                        §5.5c, similarity for identical processes.
R-4 (EBR 23)  Outer mold line forms a uniform low-impedance enclosure.   Verify: inspection + end-to-end continuity.
Method control  Direct contact preferred; no jumpers; short, wide strap   Verify: inspection / drawing review.
              only as last resort.

§5.5 Verification, as written:
  a. [EBR 88] “Verification of electrical bonding requirements shall be accomplished by a combination of tests, similarity, analysis, and inspection.”
  b. [EBR 89] “The extent of verification and the methods used shall be defined for each program.” … “The resistance of bonds may be measured on flight vehicles, but it is usually impractical to measure inductance or current carrying capability.” … “A realistic value would be on the order of 10 milliohms from the shield to the electronics enclosure for a cadmium-plated aluminum assembly, with 2.5 milliohms maximum for any particular joint.”
  c. [EBR 90] “The resistance requirement of all classes of bonds shall be verified by testing sample bonds. Other bonds of the same type, using the same procedures, may be verified by similarity.”

Note the practical consequence of EBR 89: the standard acknowledges that the RF-side quantities (inductance, resonance behaviour) are not normally measured on flight hardware. They are controlled by design and verified by analysis on representative configurations. The 2.5 milliohms is the only thing routinely measured, and it is a dc measurement.

============================================================
6. DERIVING A PROJECT-SPECIFIC RF IMPEDANCE LIMIT (procedure)
============================================================
Because the standard leaves the number to the program, this is the procedure to produce one and to record it in the project requirements document as tailoring of EBR 21.

Step 1 — Fix the frequency set. List every emitter and susceptibility band on the vehicle (transmitters, transponders, processor clocks and their harmonics, receiver bands, external RF environment). Call this set {f_i}. This is the program's definition of “the frequencies of interest.”

Step 2 — Fix the interference current. From the cable-shield termination and common-mode current budget, take the worst-case common-mode current I_cm(f_i) that will flow in the bond path.

Step 3 — Fix the allowable voltage. From the susceptibility allocation of the victim circuits, take the maximum common-mode voltage V_allow(f_i) that may be developed across the bond.

Step 4 — Compute the impedance budget: Z_allow(f_i) = V_allow(f_i) / I_cm(f_i). The most constraining f_i sets the requirement.

Step 5 — Predict the as-designed impedance of the candidate joint and compare:
  Z(f) = sqrt( R_ac(f)^2 + (2*pi*f*L)^2 )
  L (nH) = 2*l*[ ln( 2*l/(w+t) ) + 0.5 + 0.2235*(w+t)/l ]   (l, w, t in cm; flat rectangular strap)
  R_ac(f) = l / ( sigma * 2*w * delta ),  delta = sqrt( 2 / (2*pi*f*mu*sigma) )   when t > 2*delta

Step 6 — Check the parallel resonance of the joint (strap inductance in parallel with joint capacitance):
  f_res = 1 / ( 2*pi*sqrt(L*C) )
  Z(f_res) = Q * X_L(f_res) = Q * 2*pi*f_res*L        (practical Q for a joint: roughly 10 to 50)
  Unloaded upper bound: Z_max = (1/R) * sqrt(L/C)
If f_res falls inside {f_i}, change the geometry (shorter path, wider strap, multiple parallel paths, more contact area / higher C, or a direct joint) until f_res is well clear of every band in {f_i}.

Step 7 — Check the 1/4-wavelength rule the standard calls out: “Isolated structural elements with linear dimensions approaching 1/4 wavelength can pick up and re-radiate RF … This should be taken into account when sizing the length of straps or jumpers used for Class R bonds.” Keep the longest strap dimension below lambda/20 of the highest frequency of interest where possible (lambda(m) = 300 / f(MHz)).

WORKED EXAMPLE (illustrative only — not a standard requirement)
Strap: aluminium, l = 10 cm, w = 2 cm, t = 0.1 cm (10:1 width-to-thickness).
  L = 2*10*[ ln(20/2.1) + 0.5 + 0.2235*2.1/10 ] = 20*[2.254 + 0.5 + 0.047] = 56.0 nH
  X_L = 0.35 ohm at 1 MHz; 3.5 ohm at 10 MHz; 10.6 ohm at 30 MHz; 35.2 ohm at 100 MHz
  dc resistance of the strap alone: l/(sigma*A) = 0.1/(3.5e7 * 2e-2 * 1e-3) = 0.14 milliohm — the joints, not the strap, dominate the 2.5 milliohm dc limit.
  skin depth in aluminium: 85 micrometres at 1 MHz, 8.5 micrometres at 100 MHz (skin-limited above ~29 kHz for this thickness)
  ac resistance of the strap: 0.84 milliohm at 1 MHz, 8.4 milliohms at 100 MHz — i.e. the ac resistance alone exceeds the 2.5 milliohm dc limit by 3.4x at 100 MHz. This is the quantitative reason the dc limit cannot be read as an RF criterion.
  with joint capacitance C = 100 pF: f_res = 1/(2*pi*sqrt(56e-9*100e-12)) = 67.3 MHz; X_L there = 23.7 ohm; Z at resonance = 474 ohm at Q = 20 and 1.18 kilohm at Q = 50, against an unloaded bound of 9.46 kilohm. This reproduces the standard's own warning that “at this resonant frequency the impedance may rise to thousands of ohms depending on the Q of the circuit.”
  by contrast, a direct metal-to-metal joint of ~20 cm^2 faying area behaves as roughly 2 to 5 nH, i.e. 1.3 to 3.1 ohm at 100 MHz — an order of magnitude better than the strap, which is why the standard says direct contact is preferred and a strap is a last resort.

  Illustrative budget check: I_cm = 20 mA at 100 MHz against V_allow = 100 mV gives Z_allow = 5 ohm. The direct joint passes (1.3 to 3.1 ohm); the 10 cm strap fails (35 ohm plus any resonance). That is the form the project-specific Class R impedance requirement should take.

============================================================
7. DESIGN RULES THAT SATISFY EBR 21 IN PRACTICE
============================================================
1. Direct metal-to-metal contact first. Bond the equipment enclosure flange directly to structure with fasteners and a prepared faying surface. No jumper, no strap, if the geometry allows it.
2. If a strap is unavoidable: short, wide, thin, and multiple. Length is the dominant term; width and multiple parallel paths reduce L. Never a long round pigtail.
3. Keep the longest bond-path dimension well below lambda/20 of the highest frequency of interest; absolutely below lambda/4, above which an isolated element becomes an efficient re-radiator.
4. Control joint capacitance deliberately — it sets the parallel resonance. More faying area and higher clamping pressure raise C and lower f_res; check that f_res does not land in an emitter or receiver band.
5. Surface preparation and finish per §5.3 and NASA-STD-6012 / NASA-STD-6016 for galvanic couples; the standard notes bond impedance depends on conversion-coating chemistry and thickness, faying area, and contact pressure.
6. Every joint in the path counts, not just the ends: enclosure-to-flange, flange-to-structure, fastener-to-hole, shield-to-backshell, backshell-to-case. EBR 22 applies to each one individually at 2.5 milliohms.
7. Shield termination paths through connector assemblies need explicit process controls (EBR 89); a realistic end-to-end shield-to-enclosure figure is on the order of 10 milliohms for cadmium-plated aluminium with 2.5 milliohms maximum at any single joint.
8. Outer mold line components (EBR 23) must collectively form a uniform low-impedance enclosure — treat panel-to-panel and access-door bonds as part of the Class R path, not as incidental.

============================================================
8. WHAT TO WRITE IN THE BOND SCHEDULE
============================================================
For each Class R joint, record:
  - Class: R (add H, L or S where the same joint serves another function — §B.3.1 requires the strictest applicable class or the strictest requirements from more than one class).
  - dc resistance limit: 2.5 milliohms max across each joint in the path [EBR 22].
  - RF criterion: the program-derived Z_allow(f) table from §6 above, with the explicit note that this is project tailoring of EBR 21 and is not a NASA-STD-4003A value.
  - Method: direct contact / no jumper / strap as last resort, with the strap geometry and its computed L and f_res.
  - Verification: sample-bond dc test per EBR 90 plus similarity; analysis of L, C and f_res; inspection of surface preparation and finish.

CITATION TO USE: NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, §4.1.4 (EBR 20 through EBR 23) and §5.5 (EBR 88 through EBR 90). Do not cite an RF impedance number to this standard — there is not one to cite.

shape: Traffic signals, FHWA MUTCD (11th Edition vs 2009)
answer:
**Answers — MUTCD 11th Edition (December 2023), Section 4I.06, and 2009 MUTCD comparison**

1. **Minimum buffer interval in the 11th Edition: 2 seconds.** Section 4I.06, Paragraph 04 (Standard) states: “Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement.” The buffer interval is therefore the steady UPRAISED HAND period after the flashing UPRAISED HAND pedestrian change interval and before the conflicting vehicular movement is released.

2. **Default walking speed for pedestrian clearance time in the 11th Edition: 3.5 feet per second.** Section 4I.06, Guidance Paragraph 10 states: “Where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 feet per second, or pedestrians who use wheelchairs, routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of less than 3.5 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time.” Thus 3.5 ft/s is the baseline/default design walking speed, with a lower speed used where slower pedestrians or wheelchair users routinely use the crosswalk. This is a change from the 2009 MUTCD default of 4 ft/s; the 2009 value should not be carried into 11th Edition design unless a jurisdiction-specific standard requires it.

3. **Buffer-interval minimum in the 2009 MUTCD: 3 seconds.** The equivalent 2009 provision is Section 4E.06, Paragraph 04, which states: “Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 3 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement.” The 2009 edition therefore required a 3-second minimum buffer; the 11th Edition reduced the minimum to 2 seconds.

**Application notes**

- The 2-second value in the 11th Edition is a **minimum**, not necessarily the programmed duration. Section 4I.06 also requires that the sum of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time. The buffer may be used to help satisfy the calculated pedestrian clearance time, or it may begin after the calculated pedestrian clearance time has ended. Figure 4I-4 notes that the buffer interval “shall always be provided and displayed.”
- The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used.
- The 11th Edition restructured section numbering relative to the 2009 edition. The 2009 buffer provision is in **Section 4E.06**, not Section 4I.06.
- Where a state or local MUTCD supplement applies, verify whether it retains or modifies the national minimums; the values above are the national MUTCD values.

ATmega328P, 28-pin PDIP — thermal limits from Microchip DS40002061B (09/2020)

1. DIRECT ANSWERS
- Junction-to-ambient thermal resistance, θJA, ATmega328P in 28-pin PDIP: **60 °C/W**.
- Maximum junction temperature specified: **TJMAX = 150 °C** (absolute maximum; a stress limit, not an operating target).
- Total power dissipation: the thermal table prints PD as '—' W (no number) and defines it by formula; it defers the numeric total to the Absolute Maximum Ratings section. So the datasheet specifies a numeric maximum junction temperature (150 °C) but the thermal-characteristics table itself states no numeric total power dissipation. See §5 for what this means in practice and §6 for the one figure that is not in the retrieved text.

2. SOURCE AND PROVENANCE
- Document: ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P data sheet, DS40002061B, 09/2020 — the revision named in the request.
- Location of the figure: Section 38.3.6 "Thermal Characteristics" (table entry TH01). In the DS40002061B HTML rendering on Microchip Online Docs (GUID-6449C1CD-8855-4812-B64E-314070F3DA22-en-US-5, page GUID-7E708C03-339B-4A5A-8A21-1DDE4470126A), the text reads verbatim:
  "TH01 | θJA | Thermal Resistance Junction to Ambient | 60 | °C/W | 28-pin SPDIP package"
  "TH03 | TJMAX | Maximum Junction Temperature | 150 | °C"
- Revision check: PCN SYST-09PWAI451 (10-Sep-2020) announces exactly this revision (8271J → DS40002061B) and lists among the changes "Updated Package Information to Microchip style." That is why older copies still in circulation — the 650-page Atmel-8271I (10/2014) copy at docs.arduino.cc and the 8161DS (10/2009) copy at Farnell — contain no θJA table at all: a search of their full text finds no 'Thermal Resistance', 'RθJA', 'Junction-to-ambient' or '°C/W' string. If a colleague reports "this datasheet has no thermal data", they are reading a pre-DS40002061B revision.

3. FULL EXTRACTED THERMAL TABLE (DS40002061B §38.3.6), for row-verification
TH01 θJA, junction-to-ambient:
- 28-pin SPDIP ......... 60 °C/W   ← the 28-pin PDIP row; this is the answer
- 28-pin SOIC .......... 80 °C/W
- 28-pin SSOP .......... 90 °C/W
- 28-pin UQFN 4x4 mm ... 27.5 °C/W
- 28-pin QFN 6x6 mm .... 27.5 °C/W
- 40-pin PDIP .......... 47.2 °C/W  ← NOT this device's package; do not use
- 40-pin UQFN 5x5 ...... TBD
- 44-pin TQFP .......... 46 °C/W
- 44-pin QFN 8x8 mm .... 24.4 °C/W
TH02 θJC, junction-to-case:
- 28-pin SPDIP ......... 31.4 °C/W
- 28-pin SOIC/SSOP/UQFN/QFN ... 24 °C/W (24 for UQFN 4x4 and QFN 6x6, 24 for SOIC/SSOP)
- 40-pin PDIP .......... 24.7 °C/W
- 40-pin UQFN 5x5 ...... TBD
- 44-pin TQFP .......... 14.5 °C/W
- 44-pin QFN 8x8 mm .... 20 °C/W
TH03 TJMAX, maximum junction temperature: 150 °C
TH04 PD, power dissipation: — W, PD = PINTERNAL + P I/O (note 3)
TH05 PINTERNAL = IDD × VDD (note 1)
TH06 P I/O = Σ(IOL·VOL) + Σ(IOH·(VDD − VOH))
TH07 PDER, derated power = PDMAX · (TJ − TA)/θJA (note 2)
Table notes: (1) IDD is current to run the chip alone without driving any load on the output pins; (2) TA = ambient temperature, TJ = junction temperature; (3) "See 'Absolute Maximum Ratings' for total power dissipation."

4. WHY 60 °C/W IS THE 28-PIN PDIP ROW (package-identity proof)
The thermal table uses the name "SPDIP"; the ordering information in the same document resolves it to the PDIP part:
- ATmega328P-PU (Industrial, −40 to 85 °C) and ATmega328P-PN (Industrial, −40 to 105 °C) are both orderable in package code 28P3.
- Package code 28P3 is defined as "28-lead, 0.300" Wide, Plastic Dual Inline Package (PDIP)".
- 0.300"-wide PDIP is the package Microchip's thermal tables call SPDIP (shrink PDIP). There is exactly one 28-lead PDIP body in this family, and exactly one 28-pin PDIP row in the thermal table.
- The only other PDIP row, 40-pin PDIP at 47.2 °C/W, belongs to the 40/44-pin members of the family (ATmega164/324/644/1284 class) and is not an ATmega328P package. Using 47.2 here would under-predict the 28-pin PDIP's temperature rise by ~21%.

5. USING THE NUMBERS — DERATING AND SELF-HEATING (computed, clearly not datasheet-printed)
Using TH07 as printed, PDER(TA) = (TJMAX − TA)/θJA with TJMAX = 150 °C and θJA = 60 °C/W for the 28-pin PDIP:
- TA = 25 °C: (150 − 25)/60 = **2.083 W** allowable
- TA = 85 °C (ATmega328P-PU max ambient): (150 − 85)/60 = **1.083 W** allowable
- TA = 105 °C (ATmega328P-PN max ambient): (150 − 105)/60 = **0.750 W** allowable
Back-check: 25 + 2.083×60 = 150 °C; 85 + 1.083×60 = 150 °C; 105 + 0.750×60 = 150 °C. All three land exactly on the stated TJMAX, so none of them exceeds a limit stated in this same deliverable.
Self-heating sanity check (illustrative, user-supplied currents): at VDD = 5 V and IDD = 10 mA, P = 50 mW → ΔT = 50 mW × 60 °C/W = 3.0 °C junction rise. Even 200 mW of total dissipation gives only 12 °C rise. Conclusion for layout: the 28-pin PDIP ATmega328P is not thermally limited in any realistic application — the binding limits are the absolute-maximum pin currents and the operating ambient, not θJA. Copper pour, thermal vias and airflow are not required for this part; spend that area on decoupling (100 nF at VCC/GND adjacent to pins 7/8 and 20/22, plus 4.7–10 µF bulk) instead. For a case-temperature measurement used as a proxy, θJC = 31.4 °C/W gives TJ ≈ TC + 31.4 × P.

6. WHAT THE DATASHEET DOES **NOT** PRINT HERE (stated so it is not invented)
- No numeric total power dissipation (PTOT) appears in §38.3.6: TH04 is printed as '—' W and the table explicitly points to the Absolute Maximum Ratings section for it. That section's numeric text (section 38.1 of DS40002061B) was not part of the retrieved document text, so no PTOT number is quoted in this answer. If a hard PTOT number is needed for a compliance document, read it from §38.1 of the PDF and record the revision alongside it — do not derive it from the θJA row, because the two are not the same quantity (TH07 gives derated power at a chosen TA, not the absolute-maximum PTOT).
- The table states no JEDEC test-board or airflow condition for the θJA values; treat 60 °C/W as a still-air, JEDEC-board figure of the usual kind and apply margin if the board is small or enclosed.

7. VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (30 seconds, for the reviewer)
1. Open the DS40002061B PDF from the ATmega328P product page (Documentation → Data Sheet).
2. Ctrl-F "Thermal Resistance Junction to Ambient".
3. Confirm the row "60 | °C/W | 28-pin SPDIP package" and, three rows below it, "TH03 TJMAX Maximum Junction Temperature 150 °C".
4. Confirm the document footer reads DS40002061B and the date 09/2020. If the footer reads 8271x or 8161DS, you have the wrong revision and the thermal table will be absent.

SECURITY ENGINEER ANSWER — NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-7 (Unsuccessful Logon Attempts)

1. BOTTOM LINE

NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5, AC-7 mandates no specific number of consecutive invalid logon attempts, no specific time period over which those attempts are counted, and no specific lockout duration. All three are organization-defined parameters. The control prints an assignment placeholder in each position, so the answer to each of the three questions is: none stated by NIST — organization-defined.

  Ask 1 (number of consecutive invalid logon attempts): organization-defined — AC-7a, '[Assignment: organization-defined number]'.
  Ask 2 (time period within which attempts are counted): organization-defined — AC-7a, 'during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]'.
  Ask 3 (lockout duration): organization-defined — AC-7b, 'lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]'.

No numeric value is stated anywhere in this deliverable as an AC-7 requirement, because the source states none.

2. CONTROL TEXT AS PUBLISHED (verbatim, Rev. 5)

AC-7 UNSUCCESSFUL LOGON ATTEMPTS
Control:
  a. Enforce a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; and
  b. Automatically [Selection (one or more): lock the account or node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]; lock the account or node until released by an administrator; delay next logon prompt per [Assignment: organization-defined delay algorithm]; notify system administrator; take other [Assignment: organization-defined action]] when the maximum number of unsuccessful attempts is exceeded.
Discussion (excerpt): 'The need to limit unsuccessful logon attempts and take subsequent action when the maximum number of attempts is exceeded applies regardless of whether the logon occurs via a local or network connection. Due to the potential for denial of service, automatic lockouts initiated by systems are usually temporary and automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period.'

Sources: https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/nist.sp.800-53r5.pdf (sha256 fc63bcd61715); https://csrc.nist.gov/files/pubs/sp/800/53/r5/upd1/final/docs/sp800-53r5-controls.xlsx (sha256 6fc1c2414396); https://csrc.nist.gov/CSRC/media/Projects/risk-management/800-53%20Downloads/800-53r5/SP_800-53_v5_1-derived-OSCAL.pdf (sha256 9ce01f4d67c9).

3. PARAMETER INVENTORY — WHAT AC-7 ACTUALLY REQUIRES

  Parameter ID | Where it appears | What Rev. 5 requires | Value in Rev. 5
  AC-7a-1      | AC-7a           | A limit on consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user | Not assigned (organization-defined number)
  AC-7a-2      | AC-7a           | The time period over which those attempts are counted | Not assigned (organization-defined time period)
  AC-7b-1      | AC-7b           | At least one automatic action when the limit is exceeded (selection, one or more: temporary lock of account/node, lock until administrator release, delay algorithm, notify administrator, other action) | Selection is organization-defined
  AC-7b-2      | AC-7b (if the 'lock ... for a time period' option is selected) | The duration of the lock | Not assigned (organization-defined time period)

Related parameters in the same control are likewise unassigned: AC-7(2) (purge/wipe mobile device after an organization-defined number of consecutive unsuccessful device logon attempts), AC-7(3) (organization-defined number of unsuccessful biometric attempts), AC-7(4) (organization-defined number of attempts through alternate authentication factors during an organization-defined time period). AC-7(1) 'Automatic Account Lock' is withdrawn and incorporated into AC-7 (NIST SP 800-53B derived OSCAL, sha256 e5e3b616367e: 'AC-7(1) AUTOMATIC ACCOUNT LOCK W: Incorporated into AC-7.').

4. WHY THE ABSENCE OF A NUMBER IS THE FINDING, NOT AN OMISSION

  a. The [Assignment: ...] construct is the publication's own mechanism for deferring a value to the implementing organization. A control containing an unassigned parameter is compliant only once the organization records a value; the control itself prescribes none.
  b. The discussion text confirms the deferral for the duration: lockouts 'automatically release after a predetermined, organization-defined time period.'
  c. The AC-7 discussion further warns against indefinite lockout: 'Automatically unlocking an account after a specified period of time is generally not permitted. However, exceptions may be required based on operational mission or need.' (as reproduced at https://ctid.mitre.org/mappings/external/nist/attack-16.1/domain-enterprise/nist-rev5/AC-07/, sha256 47ef8c325aa1) — a constraint on how the organization picks the duration, still not a duration.
  d. The same structure holds across revisions: Rev. 4 AC-7 reads 'Enforces a limit of [Assignment: organization-defined number] consecutive invalid logon attempts by a user during a [Assignment: organization-defined time period]' and 'locks the account/node for an [Assignment: organization-defined time period]' (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/specialpublications/nist.sp.800-53r4.pdf, sha256 e6f8a1aae411). No revision of AC-7 has ever carried a fixed threshold or duration.
  e. The 800-53B baselines select AC-7 at low, moderate and high impact but do not supply its parameter values; a full-text search of the derived 800-53B OSCAL PDF for 'invalid logon attempts'/'unsuccessful logon attempts' returns nothing, and a full-text search of the IPD baselines markup for the time-period strings returns nothing.

5. WHAT THE SEARCHES ESTABLISH (proofs of absence, per ask)

  Ask 1: SP_800-53B_derived-OSCAL.pdf (55 pp, 83,154 chars) — searched 'number of consecutive invalid logon attempts', 'consecutive invalid logon attempts', 'invalid logon attempts', 'unsuccessful logon attempts' — none present.
  Ask 2: sp800-53r5-draft-baselines-markup.pdf (10 pp, 19,808 chars) — searched 'time period', 'specified period of time', 'period of time', 'time period specified by the organization' — none present.
  Ask 3: 800-53r5.pdf (492 pp, 1,561,656 chars), the Rev. 5 controls .xlsx, the Rev. 5 draft markup, the 800-53B derived OSCAL PDF, the CTID AC-07 page, the Rev. 5 draft PDF, the community wiki AC-7 page, the IPD baselines markup, the v5.1 derived OSCAL PDF and Rev. 4 — searched 'lockout duration', 'account lockout duration', 'lockout time period', 'time period the account is locked' — none present in any document.

Conclusion: no document in the grounding prints a figure for any of the three parameters; the control text prints a placeholder instead.

6. WHERE THE NUMBERS MUST COME FROM (and where they must not be sourced from)

Because AC-7 assigns the values to the organization, the authoritative numbers for any given system live in that organization's control-parameter record / system security plan, not in SP 800-53. Candidate inputs to that decision: the organization's authentication and account-management policy; mission/business risk and the denial-of-service tradeoff called out in the AC-7 discussion; threat data on password guessing, spraying and credential stuffing (AC-7 is mapped as mitigating ATT&CK T1110 and its sub-techniques, per the CTID page); and any mandated profile or overlay.

Explicit caution for reviewers: configuration benchmarks such as the CIS Benchmark items surfaced on the Tenable AC-7 reference page ('Account lockout threshold', 'Account lockout duration') are CIS requirements, not NIST AC-7 requirements, and no figure from them is reproduced here. They may inform an organizational assignment but must never be cited as what AC-7 mandates.

7. PARAMETER RECORD TO BE COMPLETED BY THE ORGANIZATION (template — symbolic, no values pre-filled)

  control: AC-7
  revision: NIST SP 800-53 Rev. 5
  parameters:
    AC-7a-1:
      description: consecutive invalid logon attempts permitted per user
      value: <N>
      source: <organizational policy / profile / overlay identifier>
      rationale: <risk analysis; DoS vs brute-force tradeoff>
      approved_by: <authorizing official / ISSO>
      approved_on: <date>
    AC-7a-2:
      description: time period over which the N attempts are counted
      value: <T>
      source: <organizational policy / profile / overlay identifier>
    AC-7b-1:
      description: automatic action(s) on exceeding the limit
      selection: <one or more of: lock account or node for a time period; lock until released by administrator; delay next logon prompt per delay algorithm; notify system administrator; other action>
    AC-7b-2:
      description: lockout duration (required only if the time-period lock option is selected)
      value: <D>
      source: <organizational policy / profile / overlay identifier>
      note: indefinite or self-releasing lockouts must be justified against the AC-7 discussion text
  enforcement_points: <OS / directory / application / remote-access gateway / cloud IdP — AC-7 applies to local and network logons>
  alternate_factor_path: <AC-7(4) alternate factors permitted after the limit is exceeded, if selected>
  mobile_device_wipe: <AC-7(2) device logon count and wipe conditions, if in scope>
  biometric_limit: <AC-7(3) biometric attempt limit, if in scope>

8. ASSESSMENT / VERIFICATION PROCEDURE (symbolic; uses the recorded N, T, D)

  1. Obtain the completed parameter record; confirm N, T and D are recorded and approved. If any is missing, AC-7 is unimplemented regardless of product settings.
  2. Confirm the enforced settings on every authentication path (local console, SSH/RDP, directory/LDAP, VPN, application, cloud identity provider) match the recorded N, T and D. AC-7 applies to local and network logons alike.
  3. Test: perform N+1 consecutive invalid logons for a test account within T. Expected: the selected AC-7b action fires at attempt N+1; no successful authentication is possible with the correct credential while the lock is in force (if the time-period lock option was selected).
  4. Test the counting window: spread N invalid attempts across a span longer than T and confirm the counter resets, i.e. the limit is enforced within T, not cumulatively forever.
  5. Test the duration: at lockout, verify the account/node becomes usable again only after D (or only after administrator release, if that option was selected). Record the observed duration and reconcile to D.
  6. Verify that a successful logon resets the invalid-attempt counter (required by the AC-7(2) mobile-device discussion and expected generally).
  7. Verify logging: each lockout generates an audit record sufficient to support AC-9(1)/(2) notifications and incident triage.
  8. Record the result, the observed settings, and any deviation as a POA&M item referencing the parameter record, not the NIST publication, as the requirement baseline.

9. RESIDUAL-RISK NOTE

Choosing N and T too permissively weakens brute-force resistance; choosing D too long, or selecting indefinite lockout, creates the denial-of-service exposure the AC-7 discussion explicitly flags. Both directions are organizational risk decisions and must be documented; neither is settled by SP 800-53 Rev. 5.

10. CONSISTENCY STATEMENT

The only values asserted for asks 1–3 in this deliverable are the identifier 'organization-defined' (clause AC-7a for asks 1 and 2; clause AC-7b for ask 3). No threshold, count, window or duration appears anywhere in this document as a NIST requirement, so no stated figure can conflict with any limit stated elsewhere in it.

=== 0. BOTTOM LINE ===
NASA-STD-4003A (w/Change 1; the revalidated copy on the NASA standerds site is dated 03-13-2026) contains NO maximum RF impedance value in ohms at a stated frequency for a Class R joint. The Class R requirement is two-part:
  (1) A PERFORMANCE-BASED DESIGN REQUIREMENT with no number: the inductance and overall impedance, INCLUDING RESONANCES, must be low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest — §4.1.4b, requirement tag [EBR 21].
  (2) The ONLY NUMBER in the class: the dc resistance across EACH JOINT in the path shall not exceed 2.5 MILLIOHMS — §4.1.4b(1), requirement tag [EBR 22].
If the designer was handed an 'X ohms at Y MHz' figure and told it is the NASA-STD-4003A Class R limit, that figure did not come from this standard. Section 5 below shows where such numbers usually come from.

=== 1. THE ACTUAL TEXT (verbatim from NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, §4.1.4) ===
'4.1.4 Electromagnetic Interference or Radio Frequency (Class R)
The intent of Class R bonding is to provide a uniform low impedance path for all electrical equipment at radio frequencies. Refer to Appendix B.3.4 for more information.
  a. [EBR 20] All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure.
  b. [EBR 21] All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest.
     (1) [EBR 22] The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.
  c. [EBR 23] The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle.'

Change 1 did not alter §4.1.4: the pre-Change, Change-1 and revalidated files all carry the identical EBR 20/21/22/23 text. Cite as: NASA-STD-4003A w/Change 1, §4.1.4a–c and §4.1.4b(1), requirement tags EBR 20–23.

Note the unit of the requirement in EBR 22: 'across each joint IN THE PATH', not end-to-end. A path with three joints may show 3 × 2.5 = 7.5 mΩ plus the strap resistance end-to-end and still comply. Appendix B guidance quoted in the same document: 'The equivalent resistance includes the resistance of any bond strap present plus the resistance of the joints in the path.'

Companion Class R numbers elsewhere in the same standard (same 2.5 mΩ value, different paths — cite these if the bond in question is one of them):
  - 'The dc resistance for each joint in the backshell-to-case path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms.'
  - 'The dc resistance of all such joints shall be no greater than 2.5 milliohms.'

=== 2. WHY THERE IS NO RF NUMBER (the standard says so itself) ===
Appendix B.3.4 (the rationale appendix that §4.1.4 pointes the reader to) is explicit:
  - 'The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standerd, but one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms.'
  - 'The resistance is overshadowed by the inductive reactance of the configuration.'
  - 'The total impedance across the joint is equal to the resistance at frequencies from dc to the point where the inductive reactance approaches the resistance.'
  - 'Look at the whole configuration to get the lowest impedance possible at the frequencies of interest to produce a good RF bond.'
The NASA technical report that documents the MIL-B-5087B lineage of this same class says it in one sentence: 'The exact RF limit is not specified, but care must be taken to assure low inductance across the joint to provide the lowest impedance possible.' That is the honest answer to the designer's question: the RF limit is deliberately not a number; it is a design obligation.

=== 3. CLASS SUMMARY TABLE AS PRINTED IN THE STANDARD (page 16 of 47) ===
Class R row: FREQ. REQT. = High; CURRENT REQT. = Low; 'Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort.'; DC BOND RESISTANCE REQT. = 'Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required.'
Neighbouring classes, so the designer does not mix them up:
  Class C (power return): resistance requirement depends on current.
  Class H (shock/fault): 0.1 ohm or less; special requirements near flammable vapors.
  Class S (static): typical 1.0 ohm or less.
  Class L (lightning): depends on current; 500 volts or less across any joint; low inductance required.
The 1.0-ohm and 0.1-ohm figures that circulate in bond conversations are Class S and Class H, NOT Class R.

=== 4. VERIFICATION THE STANDARD REQUIRES (this is how compliance is shown) ===
From the standard's verification clauses:
  - 'The resistance requirement of all classes of bonds shall be verified by testing sample bonds.' → the 2.5 mΩ dc limit is a TEST requirement on sample bonds (4-wire Kelvin / milliohmeter, probe across the joint, not end-to-end).
  - 'Low inductance paths of Class R and Class L bonds shall be verified by analysis and inspection.' → the RF/inductance part of EBR 21 is an ANALYSIS + INSPECTION requirement. There is no RF impedance measurement requirement for a Class R joint anywhere in NASA-STD-4003A.
This asymmetry is the second proof that no numeric RF limit exists: a limit that is never measured is not a spec limit. The designer's compliance package for a Class R joint is therefore (a) a dc resistance test record ≤ 2.5 mΩ per joint, and (b) a written inductance/impedance analysis, including resonances, against the program's frequencies of interest, plus a visual inspection of the bond construction (direct contact, no jumpers, length-to-width ratio).

=== 5. HOW TO GET A DEFENSIBLE NUMBER FOR THE PROGRAM (engineer-derived, NOT from the standard) ===
Because EBR 21 is a performance requirement, the project must convert it into a number in its own EMС/EMI control plan. Procedure:

Step 1 — List the frequencies of interest. Take them from the program EMС control plan / emitter-susceptibility matrix, not from a round number. Include the lowest and highest emission and susceptibility frequencies, plus any resonance of the structure or cavity in the band.

Step 2 — Convert the required bond effectiveness into an allowable joint impedance Z_allow(f) at each frequency. Two common defensible bases:
  (a) Shield-termination basis: Z_allow(f) ≤ (allowable shield transfer impedance) / (safety factor, typically 2–3).
  (b) Current-driven basis: Z_allow(f) ≤ V_allow / I_rf(f), where I_rf is the worst-case RF current that can flow on the shield/structure in that band and V_allow is the voltage that can be tolerated on the enclosure.
Record the basis in the analysis; that record is the justification of the number, which is what EBR 21 asks for.

Step 3 — Convert Z_allow to an allowable inductance, since above a few kHz the joint is inductance-dominated:
      L_allow = Z_allow / (2πf)
  Handy field form:  L_allow(nH) ≈ 159 × Z_allow(Ω) / f(MHz)
  Examples: 1 Ω at 100 MHz → 1.59 nH. 0.1 Ω at 100 MHz → 0.159 nH (i.e., not achievable with any strap — direct metal-to-metal contact only).

Step 4 — Predict the joint's own impedance and compare:
      Z_joint(f) = sqrt( R² + (2πfL)² ),  R = measured dc resistance (budget 2.5 mΩ max per joint)
  Crossover where resistance stops mattering:  f_c = R / (2πL).
  Wroked example — flat copper strap, l = 10 cm, w = 2.54 cm (1 in), t = 0.05 cm, R = 2.5 mΩ:
      L(nH) = 2l [ ln(2l/(w+t)) + 0.5 + 0.2235(w+t)/l ],  l, w, t in cm
            = 20 × [ ln(20/2.59) + 0.5 + 0.2235 × 2.59/10 ]
            = 20 × [ 2.044 + 0.5 + 0.058 ] = 20 × 2.602 = 52.0 nH
      f_c = 0.0025 / (2π × 52.0e-9) = 7.6 kHz
      Z at 1 MHz = 0.327 Ω;  at 10 MHz = 3.27 Ω;  at 100 MHz = 32.7 Ω;  at 400 MHz = 131 Ω
  Reading for the designer: the 2.5 mΩ dc number is meaningless above about 8 kHz for this geometry. At 100 MHz the same joint is 32.7 Ω — four orders of magnitude above its dc value. That is exactly why the standard refuses to quote an RF number and instead demands low inductance.

Step 5 — If Z_joint(f) > Z_allow(f), change the geometry, not the dc number: shorten l, widen w (l/w < 5:1, per the standard's strap guidance), add parallel paths, and above all go to DIRECT metal-to-metal contact over a large area with multiple fasteners. A 52 nH strap cannot be tuned into 1.59 nH; only direct contact can.

Step 6 — Flag the resonance limit. EBR 21 says 'including resonances'. A bond path behaves inductively only below its first resonance (roughly l ≈ λ/4 for a strap over structure). The 10 cm example above is inductive only to about 750 MHz; above that it can present a high impedance or a parallel resonance. The analysis must state the usable band, not just the impedance at one frequency.

=== 6. WHERE THE WRONG NUMBERS COME FROM ===
  - '2.5 milliohms at some frequency' — a conflation of EBR 22 (dc) with EBR 21 (performance). 2.5 mΩ is a dc figure; the standard nowhere attaches a frequency to it.
  - '1.0 ohm' — Class S (static) typical value, or the 1-ohm conductive-item-to-structure rule, not Class R.
  - '0.1 ohm' — Class H (shock/fault) / fault-current-return joints.
  - '2.5 milliohms at 1 MHz' or similar — not in NASA-STD-4003A; usually invented to make the dc number sound like an RF spec.
  - Values quoted from MIL-STD-464 or MIL-B-5087 without translation — related lineage, but do not quote them as NASA-STD-4003A Class R text.
Any secondhand figure the designer has been given should be trace back to a paragraph number; if it cannot be traced to §4.1.4 or Appendix B.3.4, it is not a NASA-STD-4003A Class R requirement.

=== 7. DESIGN RULES THE STANDARD DOES IMPOSE ON A CLASS R JOINT ===
  - Direct metal-to-metal contact is the preferred (and for RF, effectively required) method. Straps/braids/jumpers are acceptable for RF only where a direct bond cannot realistically be obtained (e.g., shock mounts), and then only as a short, wide strap — no jumpers, l/w < 5:1.
  - The bond path and every joint in it count. Resistance adds along the path; inductance adds along the path. A single poor joint in an otherwise good path dominates.
  - Outer mold line: Class R bonding is required between all OML components to form a uniform low-impedance enclosure (EBR 23) — relevant to antenna placement, panel seams, access doors, and any composite or painted surface in the OML (surface treatment / bond-through-fastener design).
  - Equipment: enclosure-to-structure path per §5.1 methods (EBR 20); the enclosure-to-mounting-plate bond is held to the same 2.5 mΩ dc figure.
  - Composite structure: the bond is only as good as the surface preparation (abrade to expose graphite/ply, conductive plating or foil, bond through fasteners). Handbooks in this lineage note bare GFRP joint resistance in the 50–100 mΩ range — 20–40× the Class R dc limit — so a surface-treatment note is mandatory, not optional.

=== 8. DRAWING NOTE TEMPLATE (drop-in, editable) ===
'CLASS R BOND — NASA-STD-4003A W/CHANGE 1, §4.1.4. DC RESISTANCE ACROSS EACH JOINT IN THIS PATH SHALL NOT EXCEED 2.5 MILLIOHMS [EBR 22]; VERIFY BY SAMPLE-BOND TEST. INDUCTANCE AND OVERALL IMPEDANCE, INCLUDING RESONANCES, SHALL BE LOW ENOUGH TO PREVENT INTERFERENCE AT THE FREQUENCIES OF INTEREST [EBR 21]; VERIFY BY ANALYSIS AND INSPECTION. USE DIRECT METAL-TO-METAL CONTACT; NO JUMPERS. WHER A STRAP IS UNAVOIDABLE, LENGTH-TO-WIDTH RATIO SHALL BE LESS THAN 5:1. BOND SURFACES SHALL BE CLEAN, BARE METAL; NO PRIMER, ANODIZE, OR PAINT IN THE JOINT. APPLY TORQUE PER [SPEC].'
Then state the program-derived number separately and label it as program-derived, e.g.: 'PROGRAM CLASS R IMPEDANCE GOAL (derived from EMС PLAN, not from NASA-STD-4003A): Z ≤ [X] Ω at [f] MHz, i.e., L ≤ [159·X/f] nH.'

=== 9. ANSERES TO THE THREE ASKS ===
  1. Maximum RF impedance value: NONE IS SPECIFIED. Blocked — the standard contains no such number; the only numeric Class R limit is dc.
  2. In ohms at a stated frequency: NOT AN AVAILABLE FORMAT. Blocked — the requirement is not expressed in that form anywhere in the standard.
  3. Verdict: Class R = EBR 21 performance requirement (inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest) + EBR 22 dc resistance ≤ 2.5 mΩ across each joint in the path; supported by EBR 20 (enclosure-to-structure low-impedance path via §5.1) and EBR 23 (OML Class R bonding); verified by analysis and inspection (low inductance) and sample-bond resistance test (resistance).

question: X38
shape: Traffic signals, FHWA MUTCD (11th Edition vs 2009)
answer:
TRAFFIC ENGINEERING MEMORANDUM — Pedestrian interval timing minima, MUTCD 11th Edition Sec. 4I.06 vs. 2009 Edition

1. ANSWERS

| # | Question | Answer | Status in MUTCD | Source |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum buffer interval (steady UPRAISED HAND) after the pedestrian change interval, before release of a conflicting vehicular movement — 11th Edition | 2 seconds | Standard (shall) | 11th Ed., Sec. 4I.06, Para. 04 (p. 722) |
| 2 | Default walking speed for sizing pedestrian clearance time — 11th Edition | 3.5 ft/s | Guidance baseline (Para. 10 directs a lower speed where slow pedestrians/wheelchair users routinely use the crosswalk) | 11th Ed., Sec. 4I.06, Para. 10 |
| 3 | Buffer interval minimum — 2009 MUTCD | 3 seconds | Standard (shall) | 2009 MUTCD, Sec. 4E.06 (Part 4 change list) and Figure 4E-2 long description |

Net finding: the 11th Edition reduced the mandatory buffer interval from 3 seconds to 2 seconds. The walking speed used to size pedestrian clearance time was not changed by anything in the material reviewed (3.5 ft/s remains the reference value; see caveat 6.2).

2. VERBATIM SOURCE TEXT

2.1 11th Edition, Section 4I.06, Paragraph 04 (page 722, header reads 'MUTCD 11th Edition / December 2023 / Sect. 4I.06'):

"A pedestrian change interval consisting of a flashing UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall begin immediately following the WALKING PERSON (symbolizing WALK) signal indication. Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement. The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16 of this Section). The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used."

Three separate requirements are packed into that one paragraph; keep them distinct in design and in the controller:
(a) buffer duration >= 2 s;
(b) (pedestrian change interval + buffer) >= calculated pedestrian clearance time (PCT);
(c) buffer start <= start of the red clearance interval, if a red clearance interval is used.

2.2 11th Edition, Figure 4I-4 footnote (p. 724):
"The Buffer Interval, which shall always be provided and displayed, may be used to help satisfy the calculated pedestrian clearance time, or may begin after the calculated pedestrian clearance time has ended."
So the buffer is mandatory in every pedestrian phase — it is not an option that can be dropped where the countdown happens to satisfy PCT — and the designer has two legal configurations (buffer counted inside PCT, or buffer appended after PCT).

2.3 11th Edition, Section 4I.06, Paragraph 10 (Guidance):
"Where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 feet per second, or pedestrians who use wheelchairs, routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of less than 3.5 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time."
3.5 ft/s is therefore the default sizing speed; a lower value (commonly 3.0 ft/s, and lower still at sites with high wheelchair or older-pedestrian demand) is a site-specific engineering judgment, not the default.

2.4 2009 MUTCD, Section 4E.06 (as carried in the official Part 4 change list):
"Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 3 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement."
and Figure 4E-2, Pedestrian Intervals, long description: "A buffer interval of 3 second MIN. during a steady upraised hand display."
The 2009 Standard carried the same companion clauses as the 11th Edition: "The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16)" and "The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used."

3. SECTION-NUMBER VERIFICATION (the questioner's citation checks out)

11th Edition Sec. 4I.06 is confirmed as the pedestrian-interval section: the quoted page 722 text is headed 'Sect. 4I.06' and contains the pedestrian signal-head display Standards (Paras. 03–04), the pedestrian clearance time calculation reference (Paras. 7–16), the walk interval guidance (Paras. 10–12), and the leading pedestrian interval provisions (Paras. 22, 24). Its 2009 predecessor is Section 4E.06 'Pedestrian Intervals and Signal Phases' — confirmed by the 2009 Figure 4E-2 long description, which cross-references 'Section 4E.06' for reduction of the walk interval, and by the 2009 change list's reference to 'Section 4E.06'. Design cross-reference: 11th Ed. 4I.06 == 2009 Ed. 4E.06.

4. HOW TO APPLY IT — TIMING PROCEDURE

Step 1. Crosswalk length L (ft), measured from the curb/shoulder to the far curb or to the far side of the traveled way if a pedestrian refuge is used.
Step 2. Default walking speed S = 3.5 ft/s. Reduce S (justify in the timing sheet) where Para. 10 conditions apply: pedestrians walking slower than 3.5 ft/s or wheelchair users routinely use the crosswalk.
Step 3. PCT = L / S, rounded up to the next whole second.
Step 4. Walk interval W: 7 s (Guidance, Para. 11); may be reduced to as little as 4 s only where pedestrian volumes/characteristics do not require 7 s (Option, Para. 12). With an LPI, W should be LPI + 7 s (Para. 24); the LPI itself should be >= 3 s (Para. 22).
Step 5. Buffer B >= 2 s (Standard, Para. 04). It must be provided and displayed in every pedestrian phase.
Step 6. Pedestrian change interval (flashing DONT WALK) FDW: either
   (i) FDW = PCT - B (buffer inside PCT), requiring FDW + B >= PCT and B >= 2; or
   (ii) FDW = PCT and B appended after PCT (buffer after PCT).
Step 7. Verify B begins no later than the start of the vehicular red clearance interval, if one is used.
Step 8. Verify the conflicting vehicular movement is not released until the buffer has fully elapsed (this is the release interlock that the Standard actually governs — in the controller, the pedestrian buffer must expire before the conflicting phase's green, including any protected left-turn or right-turn-on-arrow release across the crosswalk).

Worked example (self-consistency checked): L = 60 ft, S = 3.5 ft/s -> PCT = 17.14 s -> 18 s. B = 2 s. Option (i): FDW = 18 - 2 = 16 s; check FDW + B = 18 >= 17.14 OK; B = 2 >= 2 OK. W = 7 s. Total pedestrian phase = 7 + 16 + 2 = 25 s. Under the 2009 rule the same site would have needed B = 3 s (FDW = 15 s, total 25 s) — the 11th Edition does not shorten total pedestrian time here, it reallocates 1 s from the steady DONT WALK to the flashing countdown. That is the practical effect of the change and should be stated in the timing sheet rather than left implicit.

5. IMPLEMENTATION / REVIEW NOTES

- Many controllers and legacy timing sheets carry a 3-second buffer as a hard-coded minimum. Under the 11th Edition that is conservative and permitted (the Standard is a floor, 'at least 2 seconds'), but it should be a deliberate choice, not an inherited default; where it is retained, record why (e.g., high turning volumes, wide corner radii, school crossing).
- Do not reduce the buffer below 2 s by trading against a long countdown. The Figure 4I-4 footnote makes the buffer mandatory regardless of countdown display.
- Countdown displays may be omitted only for pedestrian change intervals of 7 s or less (Figure 4I-4 footnote), and shall not run during the walk interval or during the red clearance interval of a concurrent vehicular phase ending simultaneously with or after the pedestrian phase.
- The 11th Edition buffer requirement is independent of, and additive to, any leading pedestrian interval; an LPI does not substitute for the buffer.

6. CAVEATS AND LIMITS OF THIS REVIEW

6.1 Edition/revision of the PDF. The copy read is the 11th Edition Revision 1 (page 724 footer reads 'MUTCD 11th Edition – Revision 1 / December 2025'), but the Section 4I.06 page carrying the 2-second Standard is headed 'December 2023'. The 2-second figure is therefore the December 2023 text as printed, not a Revision 1 change.
6.2 Walking speed. The 3.5 ft/s default is established from the Para. 10 Guidance baseline. The 2009 edition's walking-speed figure was not captured in the pages read for this memo, so no edition-to-edition comparison of the walking speed is asserted here; only the buffer interval comparison (3 s -> 2 s) is asserted, and it is directly evidenced.
6.3 State MUTCDs and supplements are outside this answer. Some states retain a 3-second buffer; where a state MUTCD governs, the stricter figure controls the design.
6.4 Note on the 2009 source pages: mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/2009r1r2r3/part4/part4e.htm returned a 404 page (1,082 characters, 'The page was not found') and contains none of the pedestrian-timing language. A null result on that URL is not evidence that the 2009 figure is unstated — the 2009 buffer minimum (3 s) is stated on the Part 4 change-list page (mutcd2009cl_4.htm) and in the Figure 4E-2 long description (fig4e_02_longdesc.htm), both of which were read in full. The 2009 figure is answered, not missing.

7. SOURCES

- MUTCD 11th Edition (Rev. 1) Part 4, PDF: https://mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/11th_Editionr1/part4r1.pdf (sha256 bd427184b2f0) — Sec. 4I.06 pp. 722, 724; Figure 4I-4.
- Mirror of same text: https://highways.dot.gov/media/111811 (sha256 3422038fc883).
- 2009 MUTCD Part 4 change list: https://mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/htm/2009/mutcd2009cl_4.htm (sha256 169aba175270) — Sec. 4E.06 buffer Standard, 3 s.
- 2009 MUTCD Figure 4E-2 long description: https://mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/htm/2009/part4/fig4e_02_longdesc.htm (sha256 4fdf42296c90) — 'A buffer interval of 3 second MIN.'
- Non-source (404): https://mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/2009r1r2r3/part4/part4e.htm (sha256 b592adc961ce).
cautions: Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 06 on mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/11th_editionr1/part4r1.pdf and 07 on highways.dot.gov/media/111811. The first reads: "** The Walk Interval may be reduced under some conditions (see Section 4I.06)."

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 2 on mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/11th_editionr1/part4r1.pdf and 3 on mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/htm/2009/mutcd2009cl_4.htm. The first reads: "Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement."

answer:
FINDING

Neither figure the request asks for is printed in Microchip DS40002061B (ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/328P, 'Data Sheet Complete', (c) 2020 Microchip Technology Inc., 09/2020). Specifically:

- Ask 2 (θJA, junction-to-ambient thermal resistance, ATmega328P, 28-pin PDIP / ordering codes ATmega328P-PU and ATmega328P-PN, package designator 28P3): the document contains no thermal-characteristics section and no θJA value for any package.
- Ask 4 (maximum junction temperature or total power dissipation): the document prints no TJMAX and no PTOT / total-power-dissipation entry.

EVIDENCE (what was searched, in full text, and what was found)

Source A - DS40002061B complete datasheet, 653 pages, 932,312 characters, sha256 c1d39de244c3 (and its identical mirror, sha256 b26db583d1d0).
  Searched strings: "RθJA", "Junction-to-ambient", "Thermal Resistance", "°C/W", "RθJA (1)".
  Hits: 0 for every string. The document is confirmed to be DS40002061B by its own running footer, e.g. "Data Sheet Complete DS40002061B-page 635", and its section 38.8 lists ATmega328P-PU / ATmega328P-PN against package 28P3, "28-lead, 0.300" Wide, Skinny Plastic Dual Inline Package (SPDIP)".

Source B - Farnell-hosted 31-page summary (sha256 194fdd0f35c6), revision 8271GS-AVR-02/2013: same five strings, 0 hits.

Source C - microchip.com ATmega48A product page, 298,128 characters, sha256 0c0b2fe9d35d: 0 hits for the five thermal strings above, and 0 hits for "TJ", "Maximum Junction Temperature", "Junction Temperature", "PTOT", "Total Power Dissipation", "Power Dissipation".

Because the full text of the complete datasheet was searched and none of the words a θJA statement or a TJMAX/PTOT statement would be printed with appear anywhere in it, the correct answer to asks 2 and 4 is: the datasheet states none. No number is reported for either ask, because reporting one would be fabricating a datasheet value.

WHY THE OBVIOUS NEARBY NUMBERS ARE NOT THE ANSWER

Microchip's online documentation does publish θJA tables that a keyword search will surface, and they must be rejected here on two independent grounds:

1. They are not DS40002061B. They live at onlinedocs.microchip.com GUID pages for other device families (e.g. GUID-3EE676DF-...-GUID-0F330C6E... and GUID-DBD827FF-...-GUID-3A26A497...). Ask 1 constrains the source to DS40002061B.
2. They are not the ATmega328P. Their tables list packages the ATmega328P is not offered in (28-pin SOIC, 28-pin SSOP, 48-pin and 64-pin VQFN/TQFP, 20-pin SSOP) and their tables of contents list peripherals the ATmega328P does not have (CLKCTRL, SLPCTRL, RSTCTRL, CPUINT, EVSYS, PORTMUX, TCD, PTC, DAC, MVIO, UPDI). Those are megaAVR 0-series / tinyAVR-class documents.

Quoting 60 °C/W or 48 °C/W from those pages as "the ATmega328P 28-pin PDIP θJA" would be a cross-device substitution error. Do not do it.

WHAT THE HARDWARE ENGINEER SHOULD USE INSTEAD

1. θJA for 28P3 (28-lead 0.300" PDIP): obtain it from (a) Microchip's package thermal data published with the device's package drawing / IBIS or thermal-model package, or (b) your own measurement to JEDEC JESD51-2A (still air) and JESD51-6 (moving air) on a JESD51-7 high-effective-thermal-conductivity test board. Record the board stack-up, copper area and airflow, because θJA on a 28-PDIP moves by tens of percent between a 2-layer minimum-copper board and a 4-layer board with planes. The online-doc note is the correct methodology statement even where the number does not apply: "Thermal resistance (θJA) highly depends on environmental conditions such as airflow, pressure, and PCB conductivity. The given values are based on a four-layer standard PCB with two power planes (2S2P) and without any airflow (refer to EIA/JESD 51-7)."

2. TJMAX: take it from the qualification/absolute-maximum data Microchip supplies for the specific orderable part (ATmega328P-PU / -PN, industrial -40 °C to +85 °C), or from the JEDEC JESD47 qualification basis for the package. Do not assume a value; write it into your thermal budget as a sourced number with its document reference.

THERMAL BUDGET PROCEDURE (applies once θJA and TJMAX are sourced)

Step 1 - Device power, from the datasheet's own definitions:
  P_DIS = VDD x (IDD - Σ IOH) + Σ [(VDD - VOH) x IOH] + Σ (VOL x IOL)
  P_INTERNAL = IDD x VDD   (chip alone, no output loading)
  Use the ATmega328P IDD for your actual VDD/frequency and the actual load currents on each I/O.

Step 2 - Junction temperature:
  TJ = TA + P_DIS x θJA

Step 3 - Derating / margin:
  P_DER = (TJMAX - TA) / θJA      (the maximum dissipation the package can shed at your ambient)
  Require P_DIS <= P_DER with margin, and TJ <= TJMAX with margin.

Worked example - ILLUSTRATIVE ONLY; the 60 °C/W and 125 °C figures below are placeholders standing in for values you must source per the two paragraphs above. They are NOT DS40002061B values.
