answer:
# NASA-STD-4003A — Class R (EMI/RF) Bond Joints: RF Impedance Limit and Actual Requirements

## 0. Bottom line (read this first)

**NASA-STD-4003A specifies no maximum RF impedance, in ohms, at any frequency.** There is no numeric RF impedance limit in the standard — not at 1 MHz, not at 100 MHz, not at 1 GHz. A designer looking for "the number" in 4003A will not find one, and any ohm value quoted as "the 4003A Class R RF impedance limit" is a fabrication or a misreading of the DC resistance limit.

What the standard actually contains for Class R is a **two-part requirement**:

1. **A qualitative (functional) RF requirement — 4.1.4b [EBR 21]:** the bond path and every joint in it must have inductance and overall impedance, *including resonances*, "low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest." The frequencies of interest are defined by the program/equipment, **not by the standard**.
2. **A single numeric limit — 4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22]:** *"The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms."* That is **0.0025 Ω DC, per joint** — a DC resistance, not an RF impedance.

NASA-STD-4003A itself confirms that a fully compliant joint can have an RF impedance in the **ohms** range: *"The impedance of an acceptable bond may be in the ohms range for RF even though the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms. The resistance is overshadowed by the inductive reactance of the configuration."* (NASA-STD-4003A, Appendix A guidance.)

**Consequence for the designer:** the numeric RF impedance budget for a Class R joint must come from the program's EMC/EMI analysis or from a documented program tailoring — it cannot be quoted from 4003A. Section 4 below gives the procedure to derive it.

---

## 1. Document identity and revision control

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Document | NASA-STD-4003A, *Electrical Bonding for NASA Launch Vehicles, Spacecraft, Payloads, and Flight Equipment* |
| Revision referenced | NASA-STD-4003A with **Change 1** (revalidated; 47 pp). Baseline 4003A (35 pp) and historical 4003 (8 Sep 2003) also reviewed. |
| Class R definition | "CLASS R — class of bond for radio frequency current" (Definitions) |
| Clause numbering | Change 1 tags requirements as **[EBR nn]**; baseline 4003A uses 4.1.4a / 4.1.4b / 4.1.4c without EBR tags. The technical content of the Class R requirement is identical in both in the retrieved text. Cite the form your contract invokes. |
| Tailoring | 4003A §1.2 (applicability) and Appendix B (rationale for modifications/waivers) permit program tailoring. **Check the program bonding spec / EMC plan for a tailored numeric RF limit — if one exists there, it governs, and 4003A baseline no longer answers the question.** |

---

## 2. The complete Class R requirement set (verbatim where available)

| Clause | Requirement text | Engineering meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **4.1.4a [EBR 20]** | "All electrical and electronic equipment shall be bonded using the methods described in section 5.1 to provide a low impedance path from the equipment enclosure to structure." | Every box needs a defined low-impedance enclosure-to-structure path, built by the approved methods of §5.1. |
| **4.1.4b [EBR 21]** | "All Class R bond paths to structure, and the joints in that path, shall be designed such that the inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest." | The RF requirement. **Qualitative. No number. No stated frequency.** Applies to the path *and* each joint. Explicitly includes resonances (i.e., the joint/path must be evaluated above self-resonance, not just as a lumped L). |
| **4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22]** | "The direct current (dc) resistance across each joint in the path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms." | The only numeric limit on a Class R joint: **0.0025 Ω DC, per joint** (not end-to-end). |
| **4.1.4c [EBR 23]** | "The design and construction of the outer mold line of the vehicle shall implement Class R electrical bonding between all outer mold line components so as to inherently provide a uniform low impedance enclosure surrounding the vehicle." | The OML itself is a Class R bond path; seams, panels, and OML penetrations are in scope, not just box straps. |
| **Table 1** (Summary of Electrical Bonding Classes), Class R column | "Bonding resistance requirement, 2.5 milliohms or less. Low inductance required." FREQ REQMT: **High**. CURRENT REQMT: **Low**. | Confirms the split: high-frequency (RF) class, low current, 2.5 mΩ + low inductance. |
| **4.1.4.1 Electrical Connectors and Shield Termination** (baseline 4003A; 4.3.1 in 4003) | Connectors/backshells used to terminate cable shields "shall be installed to provide a low impedance path from the backshell to the equipment case"; "the dc resistance for each joint in the backshell-to-case path shall not exceed 2.5 milliohms." | Shield-termination joints are Class R joints with the same 2.5 mΩ DC cap each. |
| **[EBR 5]** | "There may be more than one purpose for bonding a specific interface, and the bond shall meet the requirements of each applicable class." | A box bond is usually Class R *and* Class H (and sometimes L) simultaneously — it must satisfy all. |
| **[EBR 6]** | "Notes shall be provided on assembly drawings indicating the applicable class or classes." | The drawing must state "Class R" and the 2.5 mΩ limit. |
| **Verification clauses** | "Class R and Class L bonds shall be verified by analysis and inspection." / "Low inductance paths of Class R and Class L bonds shall be verified by analysis and inspection." / "The resistance requirement of all classes of bonds shall be verified by testing sample bonds." / "The resistance of bonds may be measured on flight vehicles, but it is usually impractical to measure inductance or current carrying capability." | **Compliance with the RF requirement is by analysis + inspection, not by an RF impedance measurement.** DC resistance is verified by sample-bond testing and, where practical, flight-vehicle measurement. |

**Verification method note:** the standard does **not** require an RF impedance measurement on the joint, and states that measuring inductance/impedance is usually impractical. An inspector or reviewer demanding a measured RF impedance value per 4003A is demanding something the standard does not call for. (A program may add such a measurement by tailoring — see §6.)

---

## 3. Why the standard has no RF number — its own rationale

NASA-STD-4003A Appendix guidance explains the physics and explicitly forbids treating the DC limit as an RF criterion:

- "The electrical bond path between an electronic box and the structure has a complex equivalent circuit that may be simplified to a resistance in series with an inductance all in parallel with a capacitance... At higher frequencies, where the diameter or thickness of the strap significantly exceeds the skin depth, the ac resistance becomes larger than the dc resistance. The ac resistance increases with the square root of frequency."
- "The inductance is directly proportional to the length of the bond path, but is also a function of width and thickness. Multiple paths can reduce the inductance value by introducing additional parallel current paths. The magnitude of inductive reactance increases 20 dB with every decade of frequency increase."
- "The 2.5-milliohm dc resistance requirement is good for a standard, but **one should not assume a good RF bond exists just because the dc resistance is less than 2.5 milliohms.** Also, extra effort need not be made just to satisfy the dc requirement if the RF impedance is much higher due to the inductance of the configuration. Look at the whole configuration to get the lowest impedance possible at the frequencies of interest to produce a good RF bond."

Supporting NASA handbook (MSFC-HDBK-3697, *Electrical Bonding Design Guide Handbook* — **handbook, not the standard**): "The resistance of a bond joint does not change with frequency... The effectiveness of a bond at radio frequencies cannot be measured in terms of its DC electrical resistance... Measuring the DC resistance of a bond is relatively easy with a Micro-Ohmmeter, but it is impractical to measure impedance in the field. Designing for maximum metal-to-metal contact area will ensure minimum DC resistance and RF impedance."

**The arithmetic that makes the point:** for a bond path with L = 52 nH (see §4), the inductive reactance equals the 2.5 mΩ DC limit at f = R/(2πL) = 0.0025 / (2π × 52×10⁻⁹) ≈ **7.7 kHz**. Above roughly 8 kHz the DC resistance is no longer the controlling term, and by 100 MHz the same joint that passes 4003A's numeric limit with margin presents ≈ 33 Ω. That is exactly the situation the standard's qualitative clause exists to control, and exactly why it refuses to state an ohm value.

---

## 4. Procedure: deriving a defensible Z_max(f) for a Class R joint (the work 4003A leaves to the program)

Since 4003A sets no number, the designer must produce one from the program's EMI analysis and record it. Six steps:

**Step 1 — Fix the frequency set F.** Take it from the EMC control plan / EMI/EMC specification for the vehicle (the emitter and victim spectra, and the conducted/radiated test ranges that apply). *This is the "stated frequency" that 4003A does not supply; the program must state it.* Document F on the bond drawing note.

**Step 2 — Fix the worst-case interference current I(f)** that will flow through the bond at each f (shield current, common-mode current, or P-static discharge current, from the EMI/lightning/ESD analysis).

**Step 3 — Fix the allowable voltage V_allow(f)** developed across the joint (victim circuit noise margin, receiver sensitivity degradation allowance, or allowable ground-plane potential rise for antenna performance).

**Step 4 — Compute the budget: Z_max(f) = V_allow(f) / I(f).** This is the only defensible conversion of EBR 21 into ohms. Label it on the drawing as *program-derived*, not as a 4003A value.

**Step 5 — Predict Z(f) of the candidate joint.** Below self-resonance:

    Z(f) = sqrt( R_ac(f)² + (2πfL)² )
    R_ac(f) = R_dc · (1 + skin-effect factor)  — rises ~√f once t or d >> δ
    L = strap inductance (Grover bar formula, dimensions in cm, result in nH):
        L = 2·l·[ ln( 2l/(w+t) ) + 0.5 + 0.2235·(w+t)/l ]

Above self-resonance (path length approaching λ/4 at f), the lumped model is invalid — this is the "including resonances" clause of EBR 21. Use a transmission-line/full-wave model or, better, eliminate the resonance by shortening the path or going to direct metal-to-metal contact.

**Worked first-order estimates** (copper, isolated strap; ±30–50%; replace with measurement or full-wave simulation for the flight configuration):

| Geometry | L | X_L @ 1 MHz | @ 10 MHz | @ 100 MHz | @ 1 GHz |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 100 mm × 25 mm × 0.5 mm strap | ≈ 52 nH | 0.33 Ω | 3.3 Ω | 33 Ω | (lumped model invalid — λ/3) |
| 25 mm × 25 mm × 0.5 mm strap | ≈ 7.0 nH | 0.04 Ω | 0.44 Ω | 4.4 Ω | 44 Ω (near resonance) |
| Four parallel 25 mm straps | ≈ 1.75 nH ideal (2–3 nH with mutual coupling) | 0.01 Ω | 0.11–0.19 Ω | 1.1–1.9 Ω | 11–19 Ω |
| Direct metal-to-metal, large faying surface, multiple fasteners | distributed joint | mΩ-level to the first enclosure cavity resonance | | | |

Note that a *compliant* joint (2.5 mΩ DC) reads 33 Ω at 100 MHz in the first row. That is not a defect in the joint — it is the standard's own point, and it is why the last row (direct contact over large area) is the preferred construction.

**Step 6 — Iterate geometry until Z(f) ≤ Z_max(f) across all of F, then verify per §5.**

---

## 5. Compliance / verification matrix (what evidence to produce)

| Requirement | Verification method per 4003A | Evidence artifact |
|---|---|---|
| 4.1.4a [EBR 20] — low-impedance enclosure-to-structure path by §5.1 methods | Inspection | Assembly drawing with Class R note (EBR 6); bond schedule |
| 4.1.4b [EBR 21] — inductance and impedance, incl. resonances, low enough at frequencies of interest | **Analysis and inspection** (no measurement required) | Bond impedance analysis report: F, I(f), V_allow(f), Z_max(f), predicted Z(f), margin; plus geometry inspection record |
| 4.1.4b(1) [EBR 22] — ≤ 2.5 mΩ DC across each joint | **Test sample bonds**; flight-vehicle resistance measurement where practical | 4-wire Kelvin / micro-ohmmeter data, per joint, ≤ 0.0025 Ω |
| 4.1.4c [EBR 23] — OML uniform low-impedance enclosure | Inspection + analysis | OML bond drawing; seam/panel/penetration bond callouts |
| Connector backshell-to-case path | Inspection + DC resistance test | Per-joint ≤ 0.0025 Ω |

**Realistic end-to-end expectation** (from 4003A guidance): "A realistic value would be on the order of 10 milliohms from the shield to the electronics enclosure for a cadmium-plated aluminum assembly, with 2.5 milliohms maximum for any particular joint." Use this as a sanity check on an end-to-end measurement, not as a joint limit.

---

## 6. If the program needs a numeric RF impedance limit

It must be **tailored in** (4003A §1.2; Appendix B provides the rationale/waiver path). Write it into the program bonding specification or EMC plan, with three mandatory elements:

1. **The limit:** Z(f) ≤ Z_max over band f₁–f₂ (never a single number without a band).
2. **The method:** e.g., 2-port shunt-through transfer-impedance measurement on a representative joint sample using a VNA with a characterized fixture (short/open/load calibration), plus analysis for the flight configuration; or analysis-only with a defined margin.
3. **The applicability:** which joints (box-to-structure, backshell-to-case, OML seams) and whether per-joint or end-to-end.

Once tailored, the tailored value is contractually binding and the baseline 4003A answer ("no numeric RF limit") no longer applies to that program.

---

## 7. Common misreadings to avoid

| Misreading | Correction |
|---|---|
| "2.5 mΩ is the Class R RF impedance limit." | It is the **DC resistance** limit per joint (EBR 22). It says nothing about RF. 4003A explicitly warns against assuming a good RF bond from a passing DC resistance. |
| "4003A states a test frequency for the RF requirement." | It does not. It says "frequencies of interest," which the program defines. |
| "0.1 Ω is a Class R limit." | 0.1 Ω is **Class H** (shock/fault). |
| "1.0 Ω is a Class R limit." | 1.0 Ω is the **typical Class S** (static) requirement. |
| "A passing DC measurement demonstrates Class R compliance." | Compliance with EBR 21 is by **analysis and inspection**; the DC test satisfies EBR 22 only. |
| "The RF requirement applies only to the box strap." | EBR 21 covers the **path and every joint in it**; EBR 23 extends Class R to the **entire outer mold line**. |

---

## 8. Design rules that actually satisfy EBR 21

These are the constructions that make the qualitative requirement achievable (4003A Table 1 note, §5.1 methods, and NASA handbook guidance — the last two items are engineering practice, not 4003A text):

1. **Direct metal-to-metal contact over the largest practical faying area.** 4003A Table 1: "Requires low RF impedance at high frequency. Direct contact preferred. No jumpers. Short, wide strap may be used as last resort."
2. **Length is the dominant term.** Keep each bond path short; target path length < λ/20 at the highest frequency of interest, or replace one long path with several short parallel paths.
3. **Multiple parallel paths** where a strap is unavoidable (also reduces inductance and detunes resonances). NASA handbook: two straps across each shock mount at VHF and above.
4. **Finish control:** remove insulating finishes (anodize, paint, primer) from the faying surface; chromate conversion coatings are acceptable, anodize is not; use external-tooth washers or masked faying surfaces. Call out "bond after finish."
5. **Fasteners:** at least two per joint where practical; keep fastener spacing small relative to λ at the highest frequency of interest to limit aperture leakage (engineering practice).
6. **Connectors:** EMI backshells with 360° shield termination; ≤ 2.5 mΩ DC backshell-to-case per joint.
7. **OML (EBR 23):** treat seams, access panels, and antenna/radome interfaces as part of the enclosure; the requirement is a *uniform low-impedance enclosure*, not just a box strap.

---

## 9. Deliverable: drawing note that closes the gap

Because 4003A supplies no number, the drawing note must supply the program number plus the 4003A text. Recommended note:

> BOND, CLASS R (NASA-STD-4003A, 4.1.4b / 4.1.4b(1)). DC RESISTANCE ACROSS EACH JOINT SHALL NOT EXCEED 2.5 MILLIOHMS. BOND PATH INDUCTANCE AND IMPEDANCE, INCLUDING RESONANCES, SHALL BE LOW ENOUGH TO PREVENT INTERFERENCE OVER 10 MHz–1 GHz (PROGRAM FREQUENCIES OF INTEREST PER EMC PLAN XXX); DERIVED BUDGET: Z ≤ ___ OHMS AT ___ MHz (ICE-XXX). NASA-STD-4003A SETS NO NUMERIC RF IMPEDANCE LIMIT; THE FOREGOING RF BUDGET IS PROGRAM-DERIVED. DIRECT METAL-TO-METAL CONTACT REQUIRED; NO JUMPERS; SHORT WIDE STRAP ONLY AS LAST RESORT. VERIFY BY ANALYSIS AND INSPECTION; SAMPLE BONDS PER 4003A VERIFICATION REQUIREMENTS.

Fill the blanks from §4 Steps 1–4, and record the analysis as the EBR 21 compliance evidence.

---

## 10. Direct answers

- **Ask 1 — maximum RF impedance permitted by NASA-STD-4003A across a Class R joint:** none is specified. **No numeric RF impedance limit exists in the standard.** The requirement is qualitative (EBR 21). The only numeric joint limit is 0.0025 Ω DC (EBR 22).
- **Ask 2 — that value in ohms at a stated frequency:** not applicable. **The standard states no frequency** for RF impedance; "frequencies of interest" are program-defined. Any ohm-at-a-frequency figure must be program-derived per §4 and labelled as such.
- **Ask 3 — what the standard actually requires for a Class R joint:** a low-impedance, low-inductance enclosure-to-structure path built per §5.1 (EBR 20); path and joints designed so inductance and overall impedance, including resonances, are low enough to prevent interference at the frequencies of interest (EBR 21); **DC resistance ≤ 2.5 mΩ across each joint** (EBR 22); Class R bonding across the entire OML to form a uniform low-impedance enclosure (EBR 23); Class R noted on assembly drawings (EBR 6); and verification by **analysis and inspection**, with sample-bond DC resistance testing.

question: X38
shape: Traffic signals, FHWA MUTCD (11th Edition vs 2009)
answer:
Traffic Engineering Determination — MUTCD Pedestrian Buffer Interval and Pedestrian Clearance Walking Speed

Scope and units: FHWA MUTCD national text; U.S. customary units. The three requested values are:

| Ask | Requested value | Answer | Governing provision |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Minimum buffer interval in MUTCD 11th Edition (Dec. 2023), Sec. 4I.06 | 2 seconds | Sec. 4I.06, Para. 04 (Standard) |
| 2 | Default walking speed for pedestrian clearance time | 3.5 ft/s | Sec. 4I.06 pedestrian clearance time provisions; Para. 10 uses 3.5 ft/s as the baseline |
| 3 | Buffer-interval minimum in 2009 MUTCD | 3 seconds | 2009 MUTCD, Sec. 4E.06, Para. 04 (Standard) |

1. 11th Edition buffer interval — 2 seconds.
The controlling standard text in MUTCD 11th Edition, December 2023, Section 4I.06, Paragraph 04 reads: 'Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 2 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement.'
Therefore the minimum buffer interval is 2 seconds. The words 'at least' make 2 s a floor, not a recommended target. The same paragraph adds: 'The sum of the time of the pedestrian change interval and the buffer interval shall not be less than the calculated pedestrian clearance time (see Paragraphs 7 through 16 of this Section). The buffer interval shall not begin later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used.'
Figure 4I-4 in the 11th Edition labels the buffer interval '2 seconds MIN.' and notes: 'The Buffer Interval, which shall always be provided and displayed, may be used to help satisfy the calculated pedestrian clearance time, or may begin after the calculated pedestrian clearance time has ended.' Thus the 2 s buffer is mandatory in all cases, but it may be counted inside the calculated pedestrian clearance time rather than added on top of it.
Revision note: The December 2023 11th Edition text and the 11th Edition Revision 1 (December 2025) text both state 2 seconds; Revision 1 did not change this value.

2. Default pedestrian clearance walking speed — 3.5 ft/s.
The MUTCD 11th Edition sizes pedestrian clearance time using a default walking speed of 3.5 feet per second. Section 4I.06, Paragraph 10 (Guidance) states: 'Where pedestrians who walk slower than 3.5 feet per second, or pedestrians who use wheelchairs, routinely use the crosswalk, a walking speed of less than 3.5 feet per second should be considered in determining the pedestrian clearance time.' That provision establishes 3.5 ft/s as the base value and permits a lower site-specific value only where slower pedestrians or wheelchair users routinely use the crosswalk. The 2024 CDOT Guidelines for Pedestrian Signal Timing corroborate: 'The MUTCD (Section 4I.06 Clause 07) identifies that the Pedestrian Clearance Time should be based on a walking speed of 3.5 feet per second...' A walking speed of up to 4 ft/s may be used in the optional extended-pushbutton/passive-detection context (Section 4I.06, Para. 08), but that is not the default. State supplements may adopt a lower value (for example, the California MUTCD adds 2.8 ft/s where older or disabled pedestrians routinely use the crosswalk); the FHWA MUTCD default remains 3.5 ft/s.

3. 2009 MUTCD buffer interval — 3 seconds.
The 2009 MUTCD, Section 4E.06, Paragraph 04 (Standard) reads: 'Following the pedestrian change interval, a buffer interval consisting of a steady UPRAISED HAND (symbolizing DONT WALK) signal indication shall be displayed for at least 3 seconds prior to the release of any conflicting vehicular movement.' The 2009 figure (Figure 4E-2) labels the buffer interval '3 seconds MIN.' The same paragraph contains the same sum-of-intervals requirement and the same red-clearance constraint as the 11th Edition.

4. Edition-to-edition change.
The national minimum buffer interval was 3 seconds in the 2009 MUTCD and is 2 seconds in the 11th Edition (December 2023). This is a one-second reduction. Both editions use 'at least' language, both require the buffer to be displayed before release of conflicting vehicular traffic, both allow the buffer to help satisfy the calculated pedestrian clearance time, and both prohibit the buffer from beginning later than the beginning of the red clearance interval if one is used. A designer working to the 11th Edition must not carry forward the 2009 3 s value as the national minimum; a designer working to the 2009 Edition must not claim compliance with the 11th Edition 2 s value.

5. Design/verification procedure.
Let D = pedestrian crossing distance in feet; v = 3.5 ft/s by default; t_PCI = pedestrian change interval (flashing UPRAISED HAND); t_buf = buffer interval (steady UPRAISED HAND). For the 11th Edition:
- t_buf >= 2 s (absolute minimum).
- t_PCI + t_buf >= D / 3.5 s (calculated pedestrian clearance time).
- The buffer must end before any conflicting vehicular movement is released.
- The buffer must begin no later than the beginning of the red clearance interval, if used.
- The buffer is always provided and displayed; it is not optional.
- The walk interval is separate; it should normally be at least 7 s, and may be as short as 4 s under the Option in Section 4I.06.
For the 2009 Edition, replace the 2 s minimum with 3 s; the other relationships are unchanged.
Worked check (illustrative): D = 60 ft gives D / 3.5 = 17.1 s. Under the 11th Edition, with a 2 s buffer, t_PCI must be at least 15.1 s; with whole-second timing, t_PCI = 16 s and t_buf = 2 s gives 18 s and satisfies both the 2 s floor and the 17.1 s clearance requirement. Under the 2009 Edition, t_buf >= 3 s, so t_PCI must be at least 14.1 s; 15 s + 3 s = 18 s satisfies both requirements.

6. Grounding note.
The harness proof of absence for ask 1 applies only to the myboca.us page; that page is not the governing MUTCD text. The FHWA 11th Edition page read in full contains the quoted Section 4I.06 provision, so ask 1 is answered and is not listed in not_stated. No ask is blocked.

Two pages handed on give different figures for the same thing: 2 on mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/11th_editionr1/part4r1.pdf and 3 on mutcd.fhwa.dot.gov/pdfs/2009/part4.pdf. answer:
HARDWARE ENGINEERING NOTE — ATmega328P (28-pin PDIP) thermal parameters from DS40002061B

1. QUESTION AS POSED
   1) Junction-to-ambient thermal resistance θJA (°C/W) of the ATmega328P in the 28-pin PDIP (SP) package, per Microchip DS40002061B (09/2020).
   2) The maximum junction temperature TJ(max) or total power dissipation PTOT the datasheet specifies.

2. ANSWER
   Neither figure is stated on the pages that were retrieved and searched. Both asks are recorded as not_stated. No number is emitted for either, because the only θJA numbers in the evidence belong to other devices' documents and cannot be transferred to the ATmega328P, and because no TJ(max) or PTOT wattage is printed anywhere in the retrieved text.

3. EVIDENCE TRAIL (what was actually read)
   3.1 Product page https://www.microchip.com/en-us/product/atmega48a — read in full, 298,128 characters, fetched 2026-11-25T05:53:22Z, sha256 9bdcc46bd57d.
       • Search set for ask 1: "RθJA", "Junction-to-ambient", "Thermal Resistance", "28-pin PDIP", "PDIP", "°C/W" → zero hits.
       • Search set for ask 2: "TJ", "Junction Temperature", "Maximum Junction Temperature", "PTOT", "Power Dissipation", "Total Power Dissipation" → zero hits.
   3.2 DS40002061B PDF (https://www.microchip.com/content/dam/mchp/documents/MCU08/ProductDocuments/DataSheets/ATmega48A-PA-88A-PA-168A-PA-328-P-DS-DS40002061B.pdf, sha256 b9b9d83cda56; mirrored at the two LCSC URLs, sha256 c1d39de244c3 and 2e8f0dfbefbc) — the content retrieved from these fetches is:
       • §39 Packaging Information, incl. 39.2 28M1 and 39.3 32M1-A (32-lead VQFN 5x5 body S4B, Microchip drawing C04-21400 Rev A).
       • §40 Errata — a pointer to the separate document DS80000855.
       • §41 Datasheet Revision History — 41.1 Rev. B 09/2020, 41.2 Rev. A 10/2018, 41.3 Rev. 8271J 11/2015, 41.4 Rev. 8271I 10/2014.
       None of these pages carries a Thermal Characteristics table, a θJA row, a TJ(max) entry, or a PTOT figure.

4. WHY THE TWO CANDIDATE θJA NUMBERS IN THE EVIDENCE ARE NOT USED
   Two thermal tables were retrieved, but from other device documents, not from DS40002061B:
   • Table 46-8 "Thermal Characteristics" (onlinedocs GUID-DBD827FF-…): θJA = 61 °C/W (20-pin SSOP), 52 °C/W (28-pin VQFN), 48 °C/W (28-pin PDIP, SP), 52 °C/W (28-pin SSOP, SS), 33 °C/W (32-pin VQFN, RXB), 52 °C/W (32-pin TQFP, PT). TJMAX row: "Refer to the Absolute Maximum Ratings section".
   • Table 37-9 "Thermal Specifications" (onlinedocs GUID-3EE676DF-…): θJA = 60 °C/W (28-pin PDIP, SP), 47 °C/W (28-pin SOIC, SO), 67.1 °C/W (28-pin SSOP, SS), 36.1 °C/W (32-pin VQFN, RXB), 58.8 °C/W (32-pin TQFP, PT), 33.7 °C/W (48-pin VQFN, 6LX), 55.6 °C/W (48-pin TQFP, PT), 30.2 °C/W (64-pin VQFN, MR), 38.7 °C/W (64-pin TQFP, PT). TJMAX row: "Refer to the Absolute Maximum Ratings section".
   Neither package line-up matches the ATmega48A/PA/88A/PA/168A/PA/328/P family as documented in DS40002061B §39 (28M1 = 28-pin VQFN; 32M1-A = 32-pin VQFN 5x5 S4B). Different die, different die-attach area, different leadframe and different package drawing give a different θJA; the 48 °C/W and 60 °C/W entries therefore cannot be quoted as "the ATmega328P 28-pin PDIP θJA". Quoting either would be a misattribution presented as a datasheet reading — exactly the failure mode this note exists to prevent. They are listed here only so the next engineer does not re-derive them and mistake them for the answer.
   Note also that in both tables the TJMAX row is not a number: it is a cross-reference into the Absolute Maximum Ratings section. So even in a matching document, ask 2's first half resolves to a pointer, and the wattage half (PTOT) appears nowhere in the retrieved text.

5. PROCEDURE TO CLOSE THE GAP (for whoever holds the PDF)
   Step 1 — Version control first. Confirm the PDF in hand is DS40002061B Rev. B 09/2020 (§41.1 of the document itself). Earlier revisions (Rev. A 10/2018, 8271J 11/2015, 8271I 10/2014) exist and thermal/electrical content changed between them; a number quoted from the wrong revision is not verifiable.
   Step 2 — Search the PDF for the strings "Thermal", "θJA" / "RθJA", "Junction", "PDIP" and "SP". If a Thermal Characteristics table exists in the DC Characteristics chapter, read only the 28-pin PDIP (SP) row and copy the value with its footnote (board type, airflow, standard referenced).
   Step 3 — Read the Absolute Maximum Ratings section in full. Record the operating temperature range, storage temperature, any explicit "Maximum junction temperature" line, and any "Power dissipation" line. If TJ(max) is given only as a cross-reference or is absent, that is the finding — write it down as "not specified" rather than inferring one from the ambient operating range.
   Step 4 — If, as the retrieved pages suggest, DS40002061B contains no θJA at all, obtain θJA from a primary source that does: Microchip's package thermal data / packaging specification (microchip.com/packaging) for the 28-pin PDIP (SP) package, or a JEDEC EIA/JESD51-7 measurement (four-layer, 2S2P, still air) — the exact conditions Microchip's thermal tables state, together with the caveat that θJA depends strongly on airflow, altitude/pressure and PCB copper.
   Step 5 — Derate using the formulas Microchip prints alongside those tables:
       PDIS      = VDD × (IDD − Σ IOH) + Σ[(VDD − VOH) × IOH] + Σ(VOL × IOL)
       PINTERNAL = IDD × VDD            (IDD = chip current with no output loading)
       PDER      = PDMAX × (TJ − TA) / θJA
       Equivalently, the allowable dissipation at a given ambient is PD = (TJ(max) − TA) / θJA.
     No numeric substitution is performed here, because neither input (θJA for this device/package, TJ(max) from this datasheet) is sourced. Plugging in a borrowed θJA would produce a wattage that looks authoritative and is not.
   Step 6 — Record the answer with its location (section number, table number, page number) so a reviewer can verify it against the PDF, and state the revision alongside the number.

6. DESIGN IMPACT
   For a 5 V / 16 MHz ATmega328P in PDIP-28 driving light loads, dissipation is in the low tens of milliwatts (confirm IDD from the DC Characteristics table for the actual VDD/frequency), so the PDIP package has large thermal margin at 85 °C ambient for essentially any θJA in the 40–70 °C/W band. This gap is therefore very unlikely to be a design blocker, but it is a documentation gap: a thermal sign-off or a derating review (e.g. per a customer's or an internal design standard) cannot be closed with a borrowed number. Until the datasheet value is read from the correct revision, state θJA as "not specified in DS40002061B as retrieved — to be sourced" on the thermal worksheet rather than filling the field.

7. DELIVERABLE STATUS
   Ask 1: not stated — no θJA for the ATmega328P 28-pin PDIP on the searched pages (product page searched for RθJA / Junction-to-ambient / Thermal Resistance / 28-pin PDIP / PDIP / °C/W, all absent; DS40002061B pages retrieved carry package drawings and revision history only).
   Ask 2: not stated — no TJ(max) or PTOT on the searched pages (product page searched for TJ / Junction Temperature / Maximum Junction Temperature / PTOT / Power Dissipation / Total Power Dissipation, all absent; the retrieved thermal tables answer TJMAX only with 'Refer to the Absolute Maximum Ratings section').
   Nothing is listed as blocked: the evidence trail is sufficient to state that these figures are absent from the pages read, and Section 5 gives the exact procedure to obtain them from the correct source.
